title: Harvest and Choir
premise: Ada Whitlock, a pest controller in the dying farm town of Hollowmere, is called to a house where something leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. When she inherits her grandmother's farmhouse, she discovers every old photograph has gained an extra chair at the table — and the chair is slowly pulling toward the center of each frame. Ada and the ragtag neighbors she's come to love must complete the founding families' interrupted binding ritual before the thing in the photographs finishes seating itself among them; in the end, Ada takes the empty chair herself, trading her place in the world for her found family's survival, and the final photograph shows a table with one more chair and one fewer person standing beside it.
about_author: Zephyrine Eastwick is the pen name of a former rural insurance adjuster who spent a decade documenting claims in farmhouses no one wanted to enter. They write horror about the quiet violence of inheritance and live, deliberately, in a town too small to appear on most maps.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A routine wasp-nest removal at the Kessler place turns strange: clawed fingerprints on the inside of boarded windows. Ada keeps it professional, pockets a sample, and lies to herself about what she saw. Beat: uneasy competence masking denial.

chapters.title: Probate and Dust
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Her grandmother's will delivers her the farmhouse she fled at nineteen. The house smells of lavender and something underneath, like meat left in a wall. She decides to stay one week. Beat: reluctant homecoming, grief she won't name.

chapters.title: Inventory of Rooms
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada counts doors out of professional habit — eleven outside, twelve inside. The twelfth opens onto the pantry and wasn't there yesterday. She chalks its frame and moves on. Beat: dread disguised as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: The Photographs
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Sorting grandma's albums, Ada finds every family photo now includes an extra wooden chair at the table's head. In the oldest photo, dated 1911, the chair is already there. Beat: the first undeniable wrongness.

chapters.title: Neighbors
chapters.summary: Milo's POV. Teenage Milo, who mows Ada's lawn, notices her lights burning all night and brings casserole and gossip: three other houses on the road have had break-ins where nothing was taken, only moved. Beat: warmth arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Behind the pantry's false back, Ada finds the founders' ledger — six family names, including Whitlock, and a ritual described as 'the Seating,' half-finished, last entry 1911. Beat: inheritance curdling into obligation.

chapters.title: Fingerprints Again
chapters.summary: Deputy Reyes' POV. Reyes investigates the Kessler callout and finds Ada's chalk marks on a door that shouldn't exist in a house with ten rooms. She starts a file she doesn't report. Beat: institutional loyalty beginning to bend.

chapters.title: Chair Pull
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Overnight, the extra chair in the photos has migrated closer to the table's center in every image, all at once. Ada measures the distances. It is moving exactly one inch per day. Beat: arithmetic horror.

chapters.title: Dinner at Milo's
chapters.summary: Milo's POV. Milo's mother Ruthie invites Ada to dinner; the found-family thread begins. But their own family photos show the chair too, and Ruthie goes pale and says nothing. Beat: connection shadowed by shared secret.

chapters.title: What Ruthie Knows
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie confesses: her grandmother was one of the six founders, and the ritual was abandoned halfway because the founders refused the price. 'We stopped paying, so it started collecting.' Beat: truth offered, trust tested.

chapters.title: The Sixth House
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada maps the six founder houses; hers sits at the center. In the fifth house, abandoned since 1974, she finds chairs arranged around an empty space shaped like a person. Beat: the scale of the pattern revealed.

chapters.title: Reyes Reads the File
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Reyes digs into county archives: every fifty years, disappearances cluster on the road, always one per household, always someone 'who kept count.' Her loyalty to the badge frays. Beat: duty versus evidence.

chapters.title: One Inch Left
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The chair reaches the table's center in the newest photos. That night, every clock in the house stops at 3:11. Ada nails the pantry door shut. By morning the nails are arranged in a neat row on her pillow. Beat: escalation, helplessness.

chapters.title: The Choir
chapters.summary: Milo's POV. Milo hears singing from the cornfield at dusk — six voices, thin and wrong, like a hymn played backward. He records it; playback shows only wind. Beat: wonder tipping into terror.

chapters.title: Assembly
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie gathers the descendants: Ada, Milo, Reyes (whose family name was scrubbed but whose blood matches), and old Tom Voss, the last Voss heir, drunk and furious at being dragged back. Beat: the found family forms under duress.

chapters.title: Tom's Refusal
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. Tom recounts his father's death in 1974 — taken as payment when the Voss family tried to burn the ledger instead of finishing the ritual. He refuses to help. 'You don't finish a deal with that thing. You starve it.' Beat: the loyalist argument stated.

chapters.title: Loyalty vs. Truth
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Reyes confronts Ada: finishing the ritual might save the town or feed the thing forever. She demands Ada choose truth over comfort. Ada admits she's been counting doors because the ledger said the keeper must. Beat: central theme argued in a kitchen at midnight.

chapters.title: The Price, Stated
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Translating the ledger's Latin, Ruthie finds the cost: the Seating requires one founder-blooded soul to take the chair willingly, becoming the anchor that holds the thing between worlds. Beat: the bargain made explicit, hope curdling.

chapters.title: Volunteers
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Each of them privately considers volunteering. Milo offers first; Ada forbids it with a ferocity that surprises them all. Beat: love learning its own weight.

chapters.title: The Thing With Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada finally sees it — a figure seated at her kitchen table at 3:11, translucent, patient, leaving prints on everything it almost touches. It looks like her grandmother. Beat: horror made intimate.

chapters.title: It Speaks in Grandma's Voice
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The thing negotiates: finish the Seating, and it releases the town; refuse, and it collects one soul per house, starting with Milo's. Ada realizes mercy and predation wear the same face. Beat: temptation framed as kindness.

chapters.title: Tom Changes His Mind
chapters.summary: Tom's POV. Tom, sober for the first time in years, brings his family's half of the ledger and his father's notes: the ritual can be completed without a willing soul if the anchor is bound by love freely given rather than sacrifice. A loophole. Maybe. Beat: fragile hope.

chapters.title: Preparations
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. The group prepares: salt lines, the founders' six objects gathered from each house, the hymn sung forward. Small domestic scenes — cooking, arguing, patching a roof — while the corn dies in a widening circle. Beat: calm before, found family solidifying.

chapters.title: First Failure
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. They attempt the Seating early. The choir answers, the candles gutter, and the thing takes Tom's voice as penalty — he can breathe but not speak. Beat: devastating cost of improvisation.

chapters.title: Grief and Quarrel
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Blame fractures the group: Ruthie mistranslated, Ada rushed, Reyes brought the wrong relic. Milo walks out. Beat: the found family tested by failure.

chapters.title: Milo and the Cornfield
chapters.summary: Milo's POV. Alone, Milo follows the singing into the corn and finds the missing people from fifty years ago, seated in rows, alive-eyed and vacant, waiting to be called to the table. He runs. Beat: the stakes given faces.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Duty
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada deciphers the ledger's final page: the keeper who counts the doors must be the anchor — the role was always hers by blood, and grandma knew, which is why she left her the house. Beat: betrayal and inheritance reconciled into choice.

chapters.title: Grandma's Letter
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In the pantry wall, a letter: grandma stalled the thing for fifty years by counting, buying time, hoping Ada would find a better answer than she did. 'Don't pay its price. Change the terms.' Beat: grief transmuted into mission.

chapters.title: Change the Terms
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie works the translation night and day: bind the anchor not with a soul but with a covenant — six households swearing mutual keeping, renewing it yearly. It has never been tried. It might be worse than the original. Beat: desperate scholarship.

chapters.title: Regathering
chapters.summary: Milo's POV. Milo returns with the cornfield's location marked; Reyes resigns rather than let the department stop them; Tom writes his consent on paper since he cannot speak. The five assemble. Beat: broken things repaired on purpose.

chapters.title: The Last Inch
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. New photographs appear — of them, taken from inside the walls. In each, a sixth chair waits behind Ada's seat. The thing is done waiting. Beat: countdown pressure.

chapters.title: Night of the Seating
chapters.summary: Ensemble, rotating close-third. At 3:11 they begin the covenant rite in Ada's kitchen, six objects, five voices, one silence. The choir arrives at the property line. Beat: climax opening, terror and tenderness braided.

chapters.title: The Choir Enters
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The thing breaches the salt, wearing the faces of all the taken, and sits down at the head of the table uninvited. The rite falters. Beat: climax peak, apparent defeat.

chapters.title: What Milo Learned in the Corn
chapters.summary: Milo's POV. Milo realizes the seated dead aren't anchors — they're audience. The thing needs witnesses to feel real. The covenant can work if the town itself swears keeping, not just the five of them. Beat: the turn.

chapters.title: Calling the Town
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Reyes drives the road at dawn banging on every door; Ruthie calls every number in her church directory. Forty-one households swear the covenant aloud, clumsy and scared and together. Beat: collective courage, theme fulfilled.

chapters.title: Ada Takes the Chair
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The covenant needs a living keystone until the next renewal. Ada sits in the sixth chair willingly — not as payment but as host — and the thing, unfed and unwitnessed alone, thins into the photograph on the wall. Beat: sacrifice reframed as belonging.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. The corn greens again; clocks run; Tom's voice returns mid-sentence. But Ada is fainter each day, present mostly between 3:11 and sunrise. Beat: bittersweet victory, cost acknowledged.

chapters.title: Renewal
chapters.summary: Milo's POV. One year later, the town renews the covenant at a long table set for forty-two. Ada attends as a flicker in the lamplight, counted and kept. Beat: ritual as ongoing love.

chapters.title: The Photograph
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The final photograph on grandma's wall: the kitchen table, the family around it, and Ada seated in the sixth chair, smiling, permanent now — inside the frame, held by everyone outside it. Beat: resolution, haunting made homely.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Reyes' POV. Coda. Reyes visits the house, counts eleven doors outside, twelve within, and leaves the twelfth chalked and blessed. Some things you don't open; some things you keep. Beat: quiet, watchful peace.
